title: A Simple Liquid Can Stop Cavities — No Drilling Needed
summary:
A cavity does not have to mean drilling. A simple liquid, painted onto a tooth in seconds, can stop tooth decay in young children — and a major clinical trial has now confirmed it works.

The liquid is called silver diamine fluoride, or SDF. Instead of drilling out the damaged part of a tooth and placing a filling, a dentist paints SDF onto the cavity with a tiny sponge-tipped applicator. There is no drilling, no injection, and no sedation.

Dentists call this arresting tooth decay: the damaged area stops getting worse. SDF does not replace tooth material that is already lost. It works through two ingredients: silver helps fight the bacteria linked to decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the tooth's mineral structure and resist further damage.

The Phase III trial, published in JAMA Pediatrics, included 830 children younger than 6. The children were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa. Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator, said the treatment is very effective and safe, even in children as young as 1.

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Left alone, it can bring severe toothaches, infections, trouble eating and sleeping, and missed school days. For many small children, regular dental treatment is hard: some cannot sit still, and others feel real fear.

There is one tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed part of a treated tooth dark, which can show most on front teeth. The change is mainly cosmetic. For many families, skipping pain and drilling may matter more.

SDF is not new. Dentists have used it for decades in many countries, and in the United States the FDA approved it in 2014 as a medical device for tooth sensitivity. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities. What was missing was large-scale evidence from U.S. children — a key step toward FDA approval for that use.

It stops the damaged area from getting worse

background_read: A cavity is a damaged spot on a tooth that gets worse when germs keep attacking it.
Dentists usually fix cavities by drilling out the damaged part and filling the hole, which can be scary or painful for small children.
Silver diamine fluoride offers a different approach: it is painted on to stop the damage from spreading, even though it cannot rebuild tooth that is already gone.
Because it needs no drilling or sleep medicine, it can help children who find normal dental visits hard.
